hugo-studio.tagline: A single doorway to everything I build, installed like an app.
hugo-studio.role: Product owner · Design & full-stack development · Operations
hugo-studio.summary: It started with a nagging question: why does every tool I need insist on a new account? Hugo Studio is the answer — one way in, one sign-in, installed on the device like an app.
hugo-studio.techNote: The browser side is React with Vite and Tailwind. The server is Node.js with MongoDB, plus WebSocket for the wallet and instant notifications. Capacitor packages it when a native build is needed. Nothing sits on a ready-made platform — everything shares one identity layer, and that layer has to be mine to control.

highlights.title: It started as an irritation
highlights.body: The first tools were written because I needed them myself: somewhere to track work, somewhere to study, somewhere to stop for a while. The more I wrote, the clearer it became that the friction wasn't in any one tool but in the gaps between them — a separate account each, a separate sign-in, a separate place for the data.

highlights.title: So the frame came first
highlights.body: Instead of shipping more standalone products, the thing built first was the frame: one identity layer, one points wallet, one real-time notification channel, one shared interface shell. From then on a new app is content poured into the frame, not another foundation dug.

highlights.title: Installed, not fetched from a store
highlights.body: The frame runs as a PWA: full screen, an icon on the home screen, push notifications, and still usable when the connection wavers. A fix reaches people in minutes instead of waiting in an approval queue.

highlights.title: And the night shift is mine
highlights.body: One overrun of a provider quota turned out to be a loop calling an API every ten seconds. It went to five minutes, and then the architecture was split along the lines each platform actually bills for. Running it alone means owning the consequences — which is the part that teaches most.

shots.study: Learning — a staged path, graded on work you actually submit.
shots.arcade: Games — hand-written, open and play, nothing to install.
shots.services: The services page — pricing and the booking flow.

hugo-studio.closing: It grows every week. The part that matters most isn't what's on screen; it's the frame underneath — the reason the tenth app costs less effort than the first.

chanh-toa.tagline: A parish portal: mass times across 27 dioceses, the full Bible, and answers on faith.
chanh-toa.summary: Mass times change constantly and nobody announces it. Travel a little, want to attend, and you end up asking around. This site exists so that question has one place to be answered.
chanh-toa.techNote: Next.js with React and TypeScript, the interface in Tailwind, the server side on Node.js, data in Firebase and Firestore, images processed with Sharp. Posts arrive from the parish Facebook page through the Graph API. Server rendering was the choice because most of this site is material search engines need to read: Mass times, every chapter of Scripture, every question of faith.

highlights.title: The question people ask most
highlights.body: Turn on location and you see the nearest church and how long until the next Mass, across data covering 27 dioceses. Because the schedule keeps shifting, parishioners can correct it right on the card — the information stays alive through its readers, not through a one-time import.

highlights.title: Then come the questions people hesitate to ask
highlights.body: After Mass times come the things people are shy to raise in person: the sacraments, moral questions, marriage. Each has a short answer to skim, and a longer one with catechism sources for anyone who wants to follow it through.

highlights.title: The whole of Scripture, chapter by chapter
highlights.body: Old and New Testament in full, an illustration for each book, and an address of its own for every chapter so it can be sent straight to someone. The prayer section counts readings and keeps a daily streak — better at holding a habit than any reminder.

highlights.title: Wired straight into the parish page
highlights.body: The parish already posts to its own Facebook page, and nobody wants to post a second time. The server calls the Facebook Graph API on a schedule, pulls new posts and their images, compresses them with Sharp and stores them in Firestore — post once on the page and it appears in both places. The access key stays on the server, guarded by Firestore rules, and never travels down to the browser; every write must carry an administrator identity.

chanh-toa.closing: The site is live and parishioners open it daily. For a parish portal, success isn't traffic — it's that nobody has to phone around to find out when Mass is.

hwj.tagline: A fine jewellery platform priced against live gold and silver rates.
hwj.summary: A single piece costs more than a motorbike. What does the storefront selling it look like? The answer here is a magazine — large serif type, plenty of air, and not one "BUY NOW" button.
hwj.techNote: Built end to end: React and Tailwind in the browser; Node.js with MongoDB on the server for accounts, consultation bookings and the cart; product imagery on Cloudinary; sign-in through Google OAuth; and a metals API so pricing tracks live gold and silver rates.

highlights.title: It began as a doubt
highlights.body: Card grids, discount badges, red buttons — the familiar e-commerce kit was built for things bought quickly. Put it next to something considered for months and it works against the very piece it is selling.

highlights.title: So the site was built like a publication
highlights.body: Very large serif headlines, a wide grid, cream and antique gold. Products don't sit in a card grid; they sit inside an article with chapters, at the pace of an auction house catalogue.

highlights.title: Vocabulary in place of buttons
highlights.body: "Acquisition Consultation" instead of "Add to cart". "Registry no." instead of a product code. At this level, language positions a piece more than colour does, and an invitation to sit down reads better than an instruction to buy.

highlights.title: But the price can't just be beautiful
highlights.body: Gold and silver rates come straight from a market API, shown as a sell and buyback table per mace. Behind the printed page, the server side carries accounts, consultation bookings and the cart — enough for an enquiry to travel its whole distance.

hwj.closing: This was a brief I set myself, and the biggest lesson is barely technical: at this end of the market, restraint sells more than urgency.

minh-oi-media.tagline: A wedding documentary studio site — pricing, portfolio and the enquiry flow.
minh-oi-media.summary: Couples choose a wedding studio with three tabs open at once. The one that makes them message first to learn the price gets closed first. Every decision here comes out of that one observation.
minh-oi-media.techNote: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no framework at all. A page presenting five service packages does not need React; without a framework it stays light, opens fast on mobile data, and the client can edit the words in the file without calling anyone.

highlights.title: People ask the price before the name
highlights.body: The wedding trade likes to hide prices to force an enquiry. Here the five packages sit right on the path, each listing exactly what the couple receives — readers rule themselves out, or in, before anyone has to answer a message.

highlights.title: The photograph speaks first
highlights.body: The first screen is a full-bleed wedding photograph, not a slogan. For a studio, that first image is the entire proof of competence; every line of copy after it is only there to explain.

highlights.title: Portrait is the default
highlights.body: Almost everyone reads this on a phone, mid-conversation about which studio to book. So the price list folds into a single column, with no wide table to drag sideways.

highlights.title: And no framework was needed
highlights.body: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A page presenting five packages doesn't need React; without a framework it stays light, opens fast on 4G, and the studio can edit the words in the file without calling anyone.

shots.home: Home — a large photograph leads, the brand sits over it.
shots.bang-gia: Five packages, each spelling out what the client receives.

minh-oi-media.closing: Worked directly with the client, from the first requirements conversation through to handover. What they kept afterwards is a site they can look after themselves.

l3go-coffee.tagline: A coffee shop site — drinks picked by how you feel. UI/UX, with Jason Phan.
l3go-coffee.summary: A three-storey café in Cần Thơ, with a spiral staircase and walls of coloured glass brick. People choose a café by where they will sit, not by the coffee — so the site has to show the room before anyone decides to go.
l3go-coffee.techNote: React and Tailwind. My part was the interface and the experience: the colour system, the typographic rhythm, the flow through the menu, and how the photographs of the space are cropped. Jason Phan handled the data layer and deployment.

highlights.title: The room is the product
highlights.body: The spiral staircase, the glass-brick wall and the lattice of night lights are held at full size rather than chopped into a gallery. A reader needs to feel where their seat would be before caring what is on the menu.

highlights.title: A long menu nobody reads to the end
highlights.body: Sixty-eight items, and nobody reads a coffee-tea-frappé table all the way down. So the filters follow the feeling someone arrives with: need to wake up, want to settle down, staying a while with friends. Choosing by mood is faster than choosing by category.

highlights.title: My part, and his
highlights.body: Made with Jason Phan. Mine was the UI/UX: the colour system, the typographic rhythm, the flow through the menu and how the room is cropped. Building the data and shipping it was his — the line was clear from the start, so nobody stepped on anyone.

shots.khong-gian: The space page — three storeys, spiral staircase.

l3go-coffee.closing: A short project, but the clearest lesson in it: the hard part of a menu isn't listing dishes, it's helping someone stop hesitating.

m-hike.tagline: A hiking app for iOS and Android that keeps working with no signal.
m-hike.summary: Out on the trail the phone loses signal, which is exactly when it matters most. M-Hike is built around a single condition: everything has to work offline, and sync itself once the connection comes back.
m-hike.techNote: Two builds, one product. The cross-platform build is React Native on Expo with TypeScript, file-based routing through Expo Router, Leaflet maps and weather from Open-Meteo. The native build is Java with SQLiteOpenHelper and XML layouts. Both treat SQLite as the primary store and use Firebase Realtime Database to sync when there is a connection.

highlights.title: Works past the last bar of signal
highlights.body: SQLite on the device is the primary store, not a cache: creating a hike, writing notes and reviewing them all work offline. Firebase Realtime Database is only a background sync layer, so another device opens on the same trip.

highlights.title: Record what you see, where you see it
highlights.body: Every hike carries its own log: the wildlife, the state of the trail, the weather, with photos and a rating. Observations belong to the hike — delete the hike and they go with it, leaving no orphaned rows behind.

highlights.title: The route draws itself
highlights.body: GPS records distance, pace and elevation gain, then replays the walk in phases: warm-up, steady, halfway, final, done. The training plan is generated from body metrics against WHO guidance, and the app states plainly that this is general guidance, not medical advice.

highlights.title: And one button for the worst case
highlights.body: The SOS screen pulls GPS coordinates and prepares an emergency message and call, with a map link to send on. The background is pure black to preserve battery, while the screen edge flashes Morse for night search teams.

m-hike.closing: Coursework for the mobile development module at the University of Greenwich (Vietnam), built twice — native Android and React Native — to compare them properly rather than pick one on faith.
